analysis.one_liner: Expands ACA subsidies, creates a public health insurance option, and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one Democratic senator with no cosponsors, S. 352 was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a committee vote, floor vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower health insurance premiums for people buying coverage on their own, extend subsidies to middle-income families and to family members locked out of help by the so-called family glitch, and create a government-run public insurance plan sold alongside private plans. It would push the remaining states to expand Medicaid, let states cover new mothers for a full year, force drug makers to accept Medicare-negotiated prices, and ban skimpy short-term insurance plans that skip coverage rules. It also steers $10 billion a year to states, much of it as reinsurance payments to insurance companies.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance get bigger premium subsidies with no income cap; families whose employer plan is too expensive become eligible for help; uninsured adults in the 12 holdout states get new federal incentives to expand Medicaid; new mothers can be covered for a full year instead of 60 days; rural hospitals get higher Medicare payment rates; and Medicare enrollees get prescription drug prices set by negotiation instead of by manufacturers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace enrollees, uninsured adults, new mothers, seniors

how_it_helps.text: Premium tax credits are expanded: the income cap at 400% of poverty is removed and the share of income families must pay toward premiums is lowered on a sliding scale, effective in 2022 [S3].

The 'family glitch' is fixed so that family members can get marketplace subsidies when employer family coverage costs more than 9.5% of household income, rather than being judged by the employee-only premium [S3].

A public health insurance option would be sold through the exchanges, must cost no more than comparable private plans, and providers enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid could be required to participate, giving consumers a government-run alternative to private insurers [S3].

States that have not expanded Medicaid keep their full seven-year schedule of enhanced federal funding if they expand, and non-expansion states face a gradually increasing reduction in federal Medicaid administrative payments reaching 10 percentage points by 2027 [S3].
States may extend Medicaid or CHIP coverage for pregnant and postpartum women to a full 365 days after birth, instead of 60 days, with federal maintenance-of-effort conditions through 2022 [S3].
Medicare is authorized to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers by striking the 'non-interference' provision that barred negotiation [S3].
The bill forbids federal agencies from enforcing the 2018 rule that expanded short-term, limited-duration insurance plans, which can exclude preexisting conditions and skim benefits [S3].

A $10 billion-a-year State Health Insurance Affordability and Innovation Fund would pay for reinsurance, out-of-pocket help, and enrollment outreach in every state, with a federal default reinsurance program in states that do not apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers would lose the guaranteed prices that come with no Medicare negotiation. Sellers of short-term limited-duration plans lose the 2018 rule that widened their market. Hospitals and providers could be required to accept the public option's payment rates as a condition of Medicare or Medicaid participation. Taxpayers fund the $10 billion annual state fund, the larger premium subsidies, and enhanced Medicaid payments. Insurers gain subsidized reinsurance but also face a government-run competitor for customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, taxpayers, and short-term plan sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $10 billion per year, every year, from the Treasury for the state affordability fund, a large and permanent new federal cost on top of expanded premium tax credits [S3].

Much of that fund flows as reinsurance payments to insurance companies rather than directly to consumers, a design that subsidizes insurers and can lower premiums partly by shifting costs to taxpayers [S3].

Requiring Medicare and Medicaid providers to participate in the public option could squeeze providers financially, which the bill only partly addresses by giving special consideration to rural and underserved areas in payment rates [S3].

Penalizing non-expansion states by cutting their Medicaid administrative funding could reduce states' capacity to administer the program for the people already enrolled, including in the poorest states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer benefits are large and concrete: broader subsidies, a fix for the family glitch, a public option competitor, Medicare drug negotiation, and a full year of postpartum coverage. The main honest costs are the price tag — $10 billion a year for the state fund plus bigger subsidies — and the design choice that channels a large share of affordability money through insurers as reinsurance rather than directly capping what patients pay. Allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices cuts a genuine cost driver rather than adding one. On balance, the help to ordinary families outweighs the fiscal cost, but the reinsurance structure spends more than strictly needed by cushioning insurers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2021 and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Warner introduced the Health Care Improvement Act of 2021 in the Senate on February 22, 2021 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced [S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list is empty [S4].
The action history records no further steps: no committee consideration, no committee or floor vote, and no action in the House before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill covered broad ground — subsidy expansion, a public option, Medicaid incentives, and Medicare drug-price negotiation — but died without either chamber ever voting on any part of it [S2, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the pre-existing arrangements stayed in place: drug manufacturers kept their shield against Medicare negotiation, sellers of short-term limited-duration plans kept the 2018 rule, insurers did not face a public option competitor, and non-expansion states faced no new Medicaid penalty. Marketplace enrollees in expensive states and uninsured adults in non-expansion states gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, insurers, and short-term plan sellers

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only measurable support was a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of potential floor support cannot be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill entrenches insurers by routing $10 billion a year in reinsurance payments and expanded premium subsidies through them, but it also creates a public plan that would compete directly for their marketplace customers. The same bill both cushions and threatens the industry's marketplace role.

The bill repeals the 'non-interference' provision and authorizes Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices, ending the legal guarantee that manufacturers set prices without government bargaining. Seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs are the public's stake in this fight.

The bill voids the 2018 rule that expanded these plans, which are exempt from ACA coverage rules and can exclude preexisting conditions. Their business model depends on selling cheaper, skimpier coverage alongside comprehensive plans.
The bill sets a 0.85 floor on the area wage index for hospital inpatient and outpatient payments, applied without budget neutrality, which raises Medicare payments to lower-wage rural hospitals.

Providers in Medicare or Medicaid could be required to participate in the public option and accept its payment rates, adding administrative burden and rate pressure, while rural providers gain from the higher payment floor.
